title: Best Temple Stays in Korea: A 2026 Guide to a Quiet Night
description: Discover the tranquility of a Korean Temple Stay in 2026. Learn how to book, what to expect, etiquette, and top temples near Seoul for a unique cultural experience.

Why You Should Try a Temple Stay

It's easy to get caught up in the K-pop hustle and Seoul's neon glow, but ngl, sometimes you just need a pause. That's where temple stays come in. Forget the tourist traps; this is about actually experiencing Korea's deeper side. I did one last year and honestly? It was the quietest, most grounding part of my trip. You trade the idol fancams for chanting and kimchi making, and it hits different.

What Even IS a Temple Stay?

Basically, you stay overnight at a Buddhist temple. It's not a fancy hotel; it's a chance to experience monastic life. Think: waking up before dawn, meditation, communal meals, and learning about Buddhism. Some temples have more structured programs, others are chill. It's super beginner-friendly, even if you're not Buddhist. Most places give you a simple room, usually shared, with a floor mat and blanket. Don't expect Wi-Fi everywhere, and that's kinda the point.

How to Book & What to Expect

Booking is usually done directly through the temple's website or through the Korea Temple Stay website (templestay.com). Programs vary, but here’s a typical rundown. They often start around lunchtime on day one and wrap up after breakfast the next day. You'll get a schedule when you arrive. Typical Schedule:
  • Check-in & Temple Tour
  • Monastic life orientation
  • Dinner (Temple food - usually vegan!)
  • Evening meditation or Dharma talk
  • Lights out (usually around 9-10 PM)
  • Morning bell & chanting
  • Breakfast (more temple food)
  • Morning meditation
  • Clean-up & departure
Don't worry about packing much. They provide robes for you to wear. Just bring comfy clothes for sleeping, toiletries, and maybe a small towel. Oh, and any meds you need. Some temples might have specific rules about phone usage, so be prepared to disconnect. A lot of the activities are in Korean, but the vibe is usually welcoming, and many guides will help translate key parts. It's worth it. Completely worth it.

Top Temples for a First Timer

Choosing a temple can be overwhelming, so here are a few popular spots that are easier to access and have programs suitable for foreigners:

1. Jogyesa Temple (Seoul)

Location: Anguk Station (Line 3), Exit 1. Hours: Stays are overnight, check website for program dates. Take: Super central, perfect if you only have a short time in Seoul and want a taste without a long trip. It's literally in the city, but feels worlds away.

2. Bongeunsa Temple (Seoul)

Location: Bongeunsa Station (Line 9), Exit 1. Hours: Check website for program dates. Take: Right in Gangnam! You can literally see the COEX tower from the temple grounds. It's a wild contrast and surprisingly peaceful. They sometimes have English-speaking staff available.

3. Gilsangsa Temple (Seoul)

Location: Nearest station is Seongsan Station (Line 6), then a short bus or taxi ride. Hours: Check website for program dates. Take: Feels more removed from the city chaos than Jogyesa or Bongeunsa. Known for its beautiful grounds and serene atmosphere. It's a bit more effort to get to but rewards you with tranquility. Budget Tip: Stays usually run between ₩50,000 to ₩100,000 per person for the overnight program, including meals. It’s seriously good value for the experience. Etiquette Notes

Respect is key. Dress modestly (cover shoulders and knees) when in temple areas. Follow the monks' lead on behavior. Remove your shoes before entering buildings. Be quiet and mindful, especially during meditation and chanting sessions. If you're unsure, just ask! Most monks are happy to guide you.

FAQ

Q. Is a temple stay suitable for non-Buddhists?
A. Absolutely. It's about experiencing the culture and finding some peace, not religious conversion.

Q. What if I don't speak Korean?
A. Many popular temples have English information online, and some offer English-speaking guides or translation support during programs. Just being present and respectful goes a long way.

Q. What should I pack?
A. Comfortable clothes, toiletries, any personal medications, and an open mind. Robes are provided. Don't overpack!

Q. How far in advance should I book?
A. Popular temples, especially during peak seasons (spring and autumn), can book up months ahead. Try to book at least 1-2 months in advance if you can.
